chunks: Harun, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and he was asked: 'What is the matter that the adulterer is not named as a disbeliever (Kafir), while the one who neglects the prayer has been named as a disbeliever, and what is the proof in that?' So he said: 'Because the adulterer and whoever resembles him only does that due to lust, because it overcomes him. And the one who neglects the prayer does not neglect it except by considering it insignificant, and that is because you will not find the adulterer going to the woman except while he is deriving pleasure from going to her, aiming at her. And everyone who neglects the prayer, aiming at it, his aim for neglecting it is not pleasure. So when pleasure is negated, insignificance occurs, and when insignificance occurs, disbelief occurs.'

He said: 'And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked and it was said to him: 'What is the difference between the one who looks at a woman so he commits adultery with her, or looks at wine so he drinks it, and the one who neglects the prayer, to the extent that the adulterer and the drinker of wine are not considered insignificant like the one who neglects the prayer is considered insignificant? And what is the proof in that, and what is the reason that differentiates between them?'

He said: 'The proof is that whenever you enter yourself into it, it is not inviting you with an inviter, and a dominant lust does not overcome you like adultery and drinking of wine. And you are inviting yourself to neglecting the prayer, and there is no lust there. So it is insignificance itself, and this is the difference between them.'

key_terms.تَارِكُ الصَّلَاةِ: The one who neglects the prayer

ai.seo_question: Why is the one who neglects prayer considered a disbeliever while the adulterer is not, according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the adulterer and the prayer-neglector by attributing the former's sin to overwhelming lust (shahwah) that temporarily overpowers reason, while the latter's neglect stems from deliberate contempt (istikhfaf) for the ritual itself. This theological nuance highlights that disbelief in this context arises not merely from the act, but from the internal attitude of devaluing divine commandments, a key concept in Shia jurisprudence regarding major sins.
